First off - this came up in a tournament yesterday and while it did deny me a
spot in the finals and with it qualification for the EC, it didn't matter
because I needed to leave before the finals anyway, have no intention of going
to Prague and got the T-shirt anyway.

That said, this is not a whine but something that has been bugging me for,
well, probably years.

Game context:

* My predator is crippled with 4 of his 5 minions in torpor and a giovanni
weenie without dominate in his ready region along with a few 0-bleed 0-str
retainers. He is to get ousted in two turns tops.
* My prey has 1 minion with inferior dominate and 1 blood. The rest of his
minions are empty in torpor and he has no way to get them out. He has 11 pool.
* My grandprey just got his one minion Archon'd by his prey (my
grandpredator). He now has 7 pool, no minions and no permanents in play; the
smallest vampire in his uncontrolled region and crypt is capacity 7. There is
no blood on any of the ones in his uncontrolled.
* My grandpredator has a bunch of vic weenies with skillcards and intercept
retainers.and a War Ghoul. He is very low on pool (3 or 4 I think).
* I am on 9 pool, have 4 minions out (two with a .44), a fair amount of bleed
in my hand and some wake/intercept. A fairly standard Auspex-hand, so to
speak.

I'm playing a Black Hand AUS deck and have been trying to keep my grandprey
alive for a while not only so my prey doesn't get 6 more pool for me to bleed
through but also so I can grab his VP before I go heads up with my
grandpredator. So far it's working quite well; between Eagle Sight and Direct
Intervention, I have managed to get to the point where I can oust my prey
before he can oust his as described above.

In my turn I bleed my prey for 3. He knows I can't bleed for more than three
and expect him to have a deflection on hand that I can't stop him from
playing. He indeed has the deflection and sends the bleed to my grandprey,
putting him on 4 pool. It doesn't matter, because he will have to hunt next
turn and will be ousted the turn after. I bleed for 6 more, putting him on 5
pool. Even if he has a another deflection and a wake next turn, I can still
bleed him out in two actions (out of 4 available) and his prey can still
handle a bleed for 3. Yes its close, but I'm on two guaranteed ousts here.

My prey hunts, I fail to block, he discards and ends his turn.

My grandprey says: "well if I'm playing to win, I need to transfer out a new
minion" and promptly transfers himself out of the game, giving my prey 6 pool.

Now of course, under the current rules this is perfectly legal. Said player
had absolutely no way of scoring a VP short of his prey tranfering out, so he
is entitled to do whatever he wants to do. He chose to transfer out, deny me a
VP and virtually hand his prey the gamewin.

I think we all agree that doing this is rather unsportsmanlike. It would be
like rolling over to your dying predator to enforce a 2-2 split on a 4-player
table so nobody gets the gamewin which may give your friend at the other table
a good shot at the finals.

Given that the topic of transfering out has recently surfaced in a different
thread, I wondered what everyone would think about a rule that prevents people
from self-ousting.

I would personally love one, because this is one of many frustrating
situations where someone self-ousting can just completely ruin your
well-played game and it's sometimes even kingmaking.

Thoughts?

I'd love one as well and it would be easy to implement. Something like "a
player is not allowed to self-oust except if he gains a VP in the process.
This includes : using transfers during a given influence phase until the
player has no pool, paying for a card resulting in having no pool, voting in
favor of a referendum that would oust him etc." As usual, judgment would
have to be used for less obvious situations (like entering in combat with
Tension in the Ranks and both minions' controller being at 1 pool, or
something.

Sure, judgment is supposed to be used anyway, but the real net result is
that people get away with transferring out, and I see that very frequently,
these days. They also do it on purpose so that no one gets a GW. At least in
Paris, you won't play in a tournament without having at least one player
threatening to transfer out or to be kingmaker, which definitely ruins much
of the enjoyment most players expect. Cunning players will make the threat
known without hostility if they feel they could be pinned by the judge for
unsportsmanlike conduct, so that it becomes too grey to merit a sanction,
but it's still unsporstmanlike conduct. It's even done on a regular basis in
casual games, which hints at the extent to which poor sportmanship has
become the standard.

Such a rule would be easy to apply and would avoid very lame behaviours, not
to mention one less tool for the kingmakers out there.

Stone

Here's a specific example where self-ousting matters in terms of
'tactical implications.'

5-player tournament final. A -> B -> C -> D -> you.

You oust A and B. C ousts D. You reach a position where you cannot
gain further victory points. C is clearly set up to oust D, and then
you.

It is clearly in your interest to self-oust to D (creating a tie
between you and C for the win) instead of letting C oust you both
(making you lose the game.)

Is this good for the game? That's a separate issue.

> > Your grandprey opted to play in a fashion to thwart the person who was
> > clearly going to oust him, and who was clearly focused on that goal.
>
> > In a lot of places, trying your best to deny a person the VP for

We're discussing a scenario where 'not getting ousted' is specifically
not an option; all that remains is to determine -how- you get ousted,
not if.

> If
> you're self-ousting that's hardly standard play. Besides, you're still giving
> away the VP and six pool so not much VP denial there.

Again, the scenario is one where the VP will be lost no matter what
course of action is taken.

> On top of it, in the
> scenario that you're self-oust it's usually not to the guy who actually did
> the job of getting you to do so in the first place so in effect you're
> punishing someone for playing well. Where I live we call that griefing.

Sure. If your predator has not crippled you himself, it's a result of
someone else crippling you cross-table (or backwards.)

My point is that when you cripple a player who is not your prey, you
shouldn't get angry when that player decides not to roll over and
obligingly wait his turn to give you his VP on a platter as your
presumed 'reward' for your play.

Many players - when facing a deck that is successfully crippling non-
prey opponents in a clear attempt to set up (partial) table sweeps -
will immediately act contrary to the best interests of that player to
the best of their ability. LOTS of times this results in the entire
table making explicit deals to gang up on such a player until he's
ousted, then continue the game.

Self-ousting is obviously a very extreme example of playing to foil a
clearly dominant opponent, but there are occasions where it's the only
option available, and some people (as noted elsewhere in this thread,
even) think that 'good play' is avoiding creating situations where
that self-oust is their only option to retaliate against your choice
of strategy.

For instance, setting someone up with 'I have left you with one minion
that can only bleed for one, and there's just no probable way you can
win before I get around to you' frequently is reacted to less
vehemently than 'I have diablerized all your minions and you get to do
nothing but discard 1 card/turn until I get around to ousting you.'

Both might justify self-ousting, but one is more likely to provoke it
than the other.

-John Flournoy

On Jun 16, 8:22 am, "Izaak" <.> wrote:
> I think we all agree that [self-ousting when there's no reasonable chance for move VPs] is rather unsportsmanlike.

I definitely disagree. Obviously several players have also posted
this viewpoint, and I wanted to add my opinion so you realize there
are many people who think that the current rules around self-ousting
are just fine. The sportsmanship rules are specific:

1) If you have a reasonable chance at a GW, you must try to get a GW.
2) If you don't have a reasonable chance at a GW, you must try to
maximize your VPs.
3) If you don't have a reasonable chance at more VPs (or you already
have the GW), you can do whatever you want.

The self-ousting player you described was following rule #3, and it's
a perfectly good rule. Also note that "reasonable chance" can include
risk analysis. Here are a couple a good threads on that topic, if you
want to read more about it:

You can't self-oust simply because someone (your grand-predator or
otherwise) interferes with your game.

If you still have a reasonable chance at the game win or more VPs, you
can't self-oust. And the player interfering with your game may well be

He may have meant that. If he did, he's playing a different game to the
rest of us.

LSJ is quite explicit that you should be playing to win, and for the
game win if necessary. Going after your prey and *not* looking cross-
table can screw that up. As in the example I gave, stopping a turbo
deck going off may be essential to retaining a chance at the game win,
because otherwise you suddenly find Arika breathing down your neck
having just taken oodles of bleed actions, and kitted up to screw you
now too. If I just try to oust my prey in such a situation, I'm being
*stupid*.

This then becomes a question of degree. Many players will want to
secure the game win, and may want to stop ousts in the process. Or they
may want to oust cross-table, even though it doesn't help them in terms
of VP or pool. The latter mechanism is explicitly discussed by Garfield
- people might get other benefits, such as securing vote lock or
whatever. The former may be required in order to play for the game win
- though, clearly, a player may not see that, or may have a different
risk assessment, or a greater knowledge of what's left in their deck, or
whatever.

Certainly, I've seen many players over-extend themselves when trying to
control the table when, in that specific situation, I think they should
have ousted their prey and solidified their position. But the game is
not and has never been about solely surviving your predator and ousting
your prey with tunnel vision. Garfield could have created such a game,
but he didn't. There are intentional avenues for cross-table alliances
and cross-table screwing, where appropriate.

Perhaps the best example of such a tactic being flawed comes from a
discussion on rush decks. Some player - I forget who, can't have been
anyone important - suggested that the best way to win with a rush deck
was to oust your first prey, and then oust the rest of the table
backwards. Since that can be, for many such decks, a clear and
resilient strategy, being asked to play with tunnel vision is like being
asked to play with one arm tied behind your back.

Botttom-line: screwing someone other than your prey can be your
tactically strongest moves. Good players will play such moves, when
they benefit them.

Banning self-ousting is like trying to treat a broken leg with a shot of
morphine. The real "problem" is that in a game of vtes there are often
events beyond our control that can cause us to lose, or at the very least
make the game a lot more difficult.

Imagine this game:

A->B->C->D->E->

C is playing a rush deck and dunks D's first minion. D responds by not
influencing any more. C threatens B into inactivity. E takes advantage
of a lack of predator by spending most of his pool on vampires to
overwhelm A.

A has tremendous problems with her predator and her prey will not tap any
vampires and only plays defensively. This is a terrible situation to be
in. There is no way to prevent it from happening occasionally. Your
options are: adapt or die.

Never assume your predator won't have free reign to crush you.

Never assume your prey won't be on full defensive mode from go.

Never assume your grandprey won't transfer out.

Never assume your cross-table "buddies" won't harass you and try to get
you ousted.

My point here is that vtes has numerous strategic hurtles. Other players
not playing the way you'd like them to is only one of them. It's a
warzone out there. Be prepared for it.

Matt Morgan

The problem I see with that is that what is 'a smart ass' or 'mature
enough' or anything like that is a subjective judgement call, and
those are exceedingly hard to legislate and enforce.

The judge can already arbitrate on what counts as 'unsportsmanlike'
behavior. As you can see from this thread, there's a vast difference
of opinion among a number of players as to whether or not self-ousting
even should count as 'unsportsmanlike'.

Lacking a clear, concise rule that expressly forbids (at least some
types of ) self-ousting, you're left with a rule that is open to
personal interpretation among a set of players and judges that don't
agree on what the interpretation should be.

So adding a 'players should not do X' rule is a problem, both because
not everyone agrees that they should indeed not do it and different
judges would rule differently on whether or not the 'spirit of the
rule' is being violated (and different players would complain
regardless of which ruling the judge hands down.)

Making a rule that says something like "You cannot spend your last
pool on a transfer" is something that would be more clear-cut and
enforcable.

However, as LSJ noted early in the thread it's nigh-impossible to
write an enforcable, consistent rule that prevents someone from self-
ousting (or at least engineering a self-oust quickly and indirectly).

Something like "You cannot spend your last pool on a transfer" while
enforcable, doesn't stop things like "I spend all but one and invite
my predator to bleed me freely" or in-play effects or other
circumventions.

As far as the "you are not mature enough to play the game", that's a
ludicrous clause to include, considering the subjectivity of
'maturity' - I think many players know people they regularly play
against that they'd consider immature, and it's hard to justify a
maturity clause when tournament environments include pre-teen players
(especially ones with multiple tournament wins.)

It's also fairly insulting; a judge telling a player 'i'm sorry, I'm
disqualifying you because you're not mature enough to play' is just
inviting a particularly ugly argument (at least.)

Plus, how does such a player convince that same judge that they'll be
'sufficiently mature' next time? Maturity isn't a qualification for
tournament play, so you can't ban a player from future events for it.
And why codify a rule where only one singular violation counts as
'immature'? Wouldn't 'you're not mature enough to play the game' also
apply to such rules violations as 'cheating', collusion, arguing with
the judge, etc etc?

If you're going to make new tournament rules, they need to be clear,
concise, and consistent. Adding rules that rely on personal judgement
is suboptimal.

Unfortunately, self-ousting or other forms of kingmaking is a
subjective issue that is extremely hard to concisely codify, so there
may simply not be a straightforward rule to solve this percieved
problem.

As you say, you could certainly ask players to enter some sort of
social contract; however that's not something that you can easily make
a rule out of. And since there's clearly a decent number of
experienced players who feel such a contract is neither desirable nor
warranted, any unofficial contract you make is going to fail (much
like how some players have a social contract not to deal-break, yet
this does not stop other people from freely breaking deals with
them.)

Similar social contracts that most people abide by already include
stuff like 'Don't contest cards cross-table' or 'Don't diablerize
vampires cross-table _just_ because you have vote lock' or 'Don't
insultingly tell another player how badly they're playing their deck
to their face.' There's lots of players who already refuse to self-
oust if it doesn't give them a victory of some sort. Encouraging
players to continue to do so is great, and I wholly approve of that
(as well as putting social pressure on the people who do so anyway).
Codifying it (or any of the other social contracts) as some sort of
enforcable violation of a rule, however, is not something I'd approve
of.

-John Flournoy

Your grandprey can't self-oust when he/she has no reasonable chance to
win.

Your grandprey can self-oust when he/she has no reasonable chance to
win, and has no reasonable chance of improving their VPs. This includes
but is not limited to playing in a timely fashion for a time-out, which
nets 0.5VP. (That is, you can't stall, but you can make play choices
that will probably lead to a time-out - bloating, for example.)

If your grandprey is thinking about it, letting you have the VP may be
better than letting his predator have the win, because it can make the
TPs split better. You're not required to play for TPs, but there's
nothing stopping you - after all, if your position is actually truly
lost, you can choose any of the lost avenues available to you.

100% certainty is a tricky thing to achieve in practice. Some even
call it impossible. This applies to every rule in the game, not just
the example above.

Imagine you're a judge and get called to a table. Player A claims that
player B incinerated player A's Arika with a lighter and swallowed the
ashes. Player B denies this and claims that player A is a CIA-agent
trying to set him up. There are no other witnesses and both players
give a different version of the events if you try to reconstruct the
game that lead to the current game state. Should player B be
sanctioned or not?
You could make up a similar scenario concerning any specific rule (and
no need to get stuck on the absurdity, the principle of uncertainty
still applies). We must accept a degree of subjectivity if we want to
have rules at all.
